## Design decisions

1. Done gate REFUSES (not merely warns) claim-at-close, with --force as the loud escape hatch. Rationale: the brief offers 'refuse or loudly warn'; refusal is the only form that makes the pattern cost something, and the escape hatch keeps the genuinely-quick close (claim, 5s of work, done) a one-flag inconvenience instead of a wall. The refusal happens before any store mutation and before the acceptance run, so a refused close leaves the row exactly as it was.
2. Threshold 10s. The historical distribution is bimodal-ish: same-second and 1s (7 rows) are unambiguous claim-at-close; 7-8s (T370, T384) are most plausibly the same pattern with the acceptance command or two console invocations between; 11s+ starts to be defensible real work. 10 catches all nine clear cases and is a round number a worker can reason about. Documented as a named constant with the rationale.
3. Dispatch refusal keys on dispatched != null (a prior dispatch event), not on status. A second dispatch to the same row is the T376/T389/T350 shape regardless of whether the row is dispatchable, in_progress or done; the old in_progress/done warnings remain informational for rows never dispatched (e.g. recording a dispatch on an old row for the ledger).
4. The kanban-store exclusion (tasks.json/directives.jsonl/heartbeat.jsonl) is not a relaxation of the hazard rule: those files are written by managent itself on every claim/dispatch/close, so their permanent dirtiness is the live kanban's normal state. treeDirty already separates them for the same reason; the audit check now matches.
5. blocked/abandoned done rows are exempt from the audit check because the done gate never required their deliverables (T361/T379/T349 closed with literally no work). Exempting them is not a hole: a blocked row cannot later become the vehicle of a second-console edit the way a real delivered row can.
6. dispatchable rows use the exists-on-disk filter instead of exempting them, because working-without-claiming is exactly the dispatchable+dirty shape (T367's second instance). A not-yet-created deliverable is the unstarted row's normal state and must not fire.

## What I did not do

- Did NOT add a claim-time 'you are working without claiming' warning to `managent resume`/`liveness`: the audit check covers visibility and the done gate covers enforcement; adding a third surface without a brief item would have been scope creep.
- Did NOT change cmdReopen: reopening a row clears claimed and resets status to dispatchable, which is the correct dead-console recovery path and remains available (the claim-refusal message points at it).
- Did NOT touch the `--skip-acceptance` or two-phase lock machinery (T350): the gate sits before it and needs no interaction.
- Did NOT modify the live kanban beyond this row's own claim; tasks.json/directives.jsonl remain dirty with claim-side effects for the Orchestrator's regular kanban commit.

## Honest limits

- The done gate compares the CLAIM timestamp to the time the done command RUNS (nowUnix), not to the timestamp that will be WRITTEN — the write happens seconds later in phase 1. A close straddling the boundary (gap 9s at check, 11s at write) closes without --force; the check is deliberately conservative (refuses more), and the 1-second clock resolution of both timestamps dominates the error anyway.
- The audit check reads the working tree at audit time; a console that edits a deliverable and reverts it before any audit run is invisible. That is the nature of an audit, not a guard.
- The regression's control e (claim-then-done) is timing-dependent in principle (if the machine took >10s between the two commands the refusal would not fire); in practice the two commands are back-to-back sub-second invocations. All 12 controls passed on every run.
- Full zig build test stays red on the documented pre-existing engine failures (vb_bellman_4x4, qa023_brute_2x2, differential/calibration); this change's own steps all pass.
